lessons.summary: Trace a design decision from an evidenced need through specification, creation and evaluation.
objectives: Use test evidence to justify iteration.
keyIdeas: A design problem belongs to a user in a context.
Specifications must be testable.
Evaluation compares evidence with criteria rather than describing the final product.

definitions.meaning: A measurable requirement used to guide and evaluate a solution.
A representation built to test selected aspects of a proposed solution.
A change made in response to evidence from testing or feedback.

method: Define user, context and observed problem.
Prioritise research questions.
Translate evidence into measurable criteria.
Prototype risky assumptions early and record why each revision occurs.

workedExample.prompt: Improve “The bottle should be easy to use” as a specification.
steps: Name the user and action.
Choose a measurable threshold.
State a test.
workedExample.conclusion: “A Year 5 learner wearing gloves can open and reseal the bottle within 8 seconds in four of five trials” is testable and user-specific.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating a feature list as a specification.
misconceptions.correction: Each important requirement needs a measurable condition and test.

misconceptions.mistake: Changing a design without recording why.
misconceptions.correction: Link every iteration to evidence, a failed criterion or new constraint.

practice.prompt: Write two measurable criteria for a reusable lunch container.
solution: Example: no leakage after 30 seconds upside down; mass below 450 g when empty.

practice.prompt: Explain why interviewing one user and observing the task can provide different evidence.
hints: Compare reported preference with observed behaviour.
solution: An interview reveals priorities and explanations.
Observation can expose actions or difficulties the user does not mention.
Together they reduce reliance on one evidence type.

practice.prompt: A prototype passes strength tests but users avoid it. Evaluate the next design step.
hints: Technical success is not complete success.
solution: Retain the validated structural decisions.
Investigate usability, appearance, effort and context through targeted observation or interviews.
Revise features that fail the criteria and test the changed prototype with representative users; change a criterion only when new evidence justifies it.

practice.prompt: A team says “We completed the cycle because we built the model.” Explain the missing evidence.
hints: Ask whether the need was met.
solution: The model demonstrates creation.
The team still needs tests against its specifications.
It should use results to evaluate success and identify any justified revision.
successCriteria: The team still needs tests against its specifications.
It should use results to evaluate success and identify any justified revision.

practice.prompt: A prototype passes a size test but confuses users. Explain why returning to research is reasonable.
solution: Passing the size criterion establishes only fit.
Observed confusion suggests a usability need remains unresolved.
Further observation can identify whether labels, arrangement or instructions need revision.
successCriteria: Passing the size criterion establishes only fit.
Observed confusion suggests a usability need remains unresolved.
Further observation can identify whether labels, arrangement or instructions need revision.

checklist: I define a real user and context.
Every iteration has an evidence trail.

notes.title: Design cycle in context
paragraphs: The design cycle connects inquiry, development, creation and evaluation through decisions supported by evidence. It is not a rule that each stage happens only once. A failed usability test may reveal an unclear requirement, sending the designer back to inquiry before making another prototype. Keep the problem separate from a favoured solution so alternatives remain possible. At each transition, record what was learned and why the next action follows. A finished object is evidence of making; meeting the agreed criteria requires separate evaluation.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional case: a classroom sign is attractive, but four of six visitors cannot find the collection tray. Decide the next design step.
steps: The finding concerns navigation, so appearance alone does not demonstrate success.
Observe where visitors look and compare the sign’s wording and placement before revising a prototype.
workedExamples.conclusion: Return to the evidence behind the navigation requirement, then test a targeted change with the same task.

flashcards.front: Why can a design stage be revisited?
flashcards.back: New evidence can reveal a problem in an earlier assumption or decision.

flashcards.front: How does an object differ from an evaluated outcome?
flashcards.back: The object shows it was made; evaluation checks it against requirements.

flashcards.front: Why separate problem and solution?
flashcards.back: It keeps alternative ways of meeting the need open.

flashcards.front: What belongs in a decision record?
flashcards.back: Evidence, the decision it supports and the next action.

lessons.summary: Choose the smallest prototype that can test the riskiest design assumption, then turn observations into traceable revisions.
objectives: Match prototype fidelity to a test question.
Collect observable evidence against a criterion.
Document a justified iteration without rewriting the original result.
keyIdeas: A prototype is an experiment, not a miniature final product.
High fidelity is useful only when detail is necessary for the decision.
A failed test is valuable when it reveals what to change and why.

definitions.meaning: How closely a prototype represents the appearance, behaviour or materials of the intended solution.
An observed attempt by a representative user to complete defined tasks with a design.
A dated record linking evidence, interpretation and a design change.

method: Name one uncertain assumption.
Choose a prototype that exposes that uncertainty with minimum unnecessary detail.
Define task, participant, measure and success threshold before testing.
Record observations separately from interpretations.
Keep the original result and add a dated revision decision.

workedExample.prompt: A team is unsure whether learners can find homework in a proposed app navigation.
steps: The risk is information architecture, not colour or animation.
Create a clickable greyscale path with realistic labels.
Ask representative learners to find and open a named homework task without coaching.
Record completion, route taken, errors and hesitation.
Revise labels or grouping only after comparing evidence with the threshold.
workedExample.conclusion: A focused low-fidelity test answers the navigation question faster and more clearly than polishing the entire interface.

misconceptions.mistake: Making every prototype look finished.
misconceptions.correction: Use only the fidelity needed to test the current decision.

misconceptions.mistake: Asking users whether they like the design instead of observing a task.
misconceptions.correction: Pair opinions with behaviour, completion evidence and follow-up questions.

practice.prompt: Select a suitable prototype for testing whether a bottle grip fits different hand sizes.
hints: The test concerns dimensions and handling.
solution: Use an adjustable or quickly fabricated physical grip model.
A screen drawing cannot provide handling evidence.

practice.prompt: Design a usability test for a school-library search prototype.
hints: Define task, participant, measure and threshold.
solution: Recruit representative learners.
Give each learner the same book-finding task without hints.
Record completion, time, wrong turns and comments.
Set a threshold such as four of five learners completing within two minutes.

practice.prompt: The predeclared target is at least four of five users completing the core task independently. A polished prototype receives positive comments, but three of five users fail the core task. Evaluate the next step.
hints: Task evidence and appearance feedback answer different questions.
solution: Positive comments support aspects of presentation but do not establish usability.
The failure rate misses the core-task threshold.
Inspect failure paths, revise the responsible interaction, preserve the test record and rerun the same task before adding polish.

practice.prompt: A foam chair model is used to claim the final chair is safe under load. Evaluate.
solution: The foam model may represent shape or scale.
It does not establish the load-bearing behaviour of the final materials and joints.
A suitable strength evaluation under appropriate supervision is needed before making a safety claim.
successCriteria: The foam model may represent shape or scale.
It does not establish the load-bearing behaviour of the final materials and joints.
A suitable strength evaluation under appropriate supervision is needed before making a safety claim.

practice.prompt: A team spends hours colouring a prototype intended only to test label clarity. Suggest a better allocation.
solution: Keep labels readable and the layout realistic enough for the task.
Use simple visual styling where colour is not part of the test question.
Spend the saved time observing several users and revising ambiguous wording.
successCriteria: Keep labels readable and the layout realistic enough for the task.
Use simple visual styling where colour is not part of the test question.
Spend the saved time observing several users and revising ambiguous wording.

checklist: My revision cites the evidence that caused it.

notes.title: Prototyping in context
paragraphs: A prototype is built to answer a question at a chosen level of detail. A paper screen can test whether labels make sense without implementing a database. A card mock-up can test reach and arrangement without proving final strength. State the uncertainty before choosing materials or fidelity. Keep features irrelevant to the test simple so time is spent on what the result can actually establish. Record limitations explicitly: success with a simplified model does not automatically transfer to a finished product with different dimensions, materials or interaction.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional task: test whether a new user understands three menu labels before programming an app.
steps: Create paper screens with the proposed labels and a realistic task, such as finding the next club meeting.
Ask a participant to choose a route without coaching, recording wrong turns and comments.
workedExamples.conclusion: The prototype can reveal label and navigation problems, but it does not test loading speed or real data storage.

flashcards.front: What should determine prototype fidelity?
flashcards.back: The uncertainty the prototype needs to investigate.

flashcards.front: What can a paper interface test?
flashcards.back: Labels, task flow and some navigation decisions.

flashcards.front: What can it not establish by itself?
flashcards.back: Technical performance, real data handling or all final interaction behaviour.

flashcards.front: Why avoid coaching during a usability trial?
flashcards.back: Coaching can hide the difficulty the prototype is meant to reveal.

diagrams.description: Uncertainty → Prototype → Observation. The task produces evidence about the chosen uncertainty.

nodes.label: Prototype
nodes.detail: Paper screens with clickable choices simulated by hand.

lessons.summary: Frame a specific user difficulty before choosing a product.
objectives: Separate a need from a proposed solution.
Use observations to define a bounded problem.
Write a brief with users, context and constraints.
explanation: A design problem describes a gap between what people need to do and what happens in a particular context. “Make an app” selects a solution before showing a need. “New visitors cannot locate the book return point without asking staff” identifies people, a task and a difficulty to investigate. Distinguish an observation from its possible cause: stopping at a junction does not prove that someone cannot read a sign.

Define a manageable scope using evidence and practical constraints. In an original hypothetical library case, three of five first-time visitors asked where to return books. This motivates investigation; it is not a population-wide failure rate or proof that a new sign will help. A useful brief states the outcome sought, the setting and limits while leaving room for different solutions. Revisit the brief when research challenges the first explanation.
keyIdeas: State the user goal before the artefact.
Separate assumptions from observations.
A small sample does not establish prevalence.

definitions.meaning: An outcome a user must achieve in a context.
A limit such as space, time or available materials.
A concise statement of the problem, users, intended outcome and scope.

method: Describe the observed task and difficulty.
Record who, where and when without identifying individuals.
List plausible explanations and missing evidence.
Write a solution-open brief with constraints.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical evidence: three of five first-time library visitors asked staff where to return books. The entrance noticeboard is crowded. Write a brief.
steps: Identify the user and goal: first-time visitors returning books.
Asking for directions was observed; clutter causing it is a hypothesis.
Specify the outcome within the existing entrance area, with no construction.
Leave placement, wording and other possible solutions open until research.
workedExample.conclusion: Investigate how to help first-time visitors find the return point independently within the existing entrance layout.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling “build a kiosk” the need.
misconceptions.correction: A kiosk is a proposed solution; describe the task first.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating five observations as proof about everyone.
misconceptions.correction: Report the sample and context; investigate other users and circumstances.

practice.prompt: Rewrite “Our school needs a new organiser app” as a user-centred problem. Hypothetical evidence: four of six interviewed pupils could not locate the current homework deadline.
hints: Name the task and observed difficulty.
solution: Some interviewed pupils could not locate the current homework deadline; investigate how pupils can find the correct deadline when planning work.
These interviews do not establish that all pupils have the problem or that an app is necessary.

practice.prompt: In a hypothetical corridor two visitors pause at a junction; a designer writes “They cannot understand English.” Separate observation from inference and propose a follow-up.
solution: The observation is that two visitors paused. Language understanding is an untested inference.
Ask what they were trying to do and observe how they use the directions; they may simply be waiting.

practice.prompt: Write a brief for a hypothetical classroom where shared scissors are hard to find. There is 200 mm of shelf width and only card and tape for a first prototype. Include a limitation if only one class was observed.
hints: State goal, users, context and limits.
solution: Help pupils locate and return shared scissors using a first prototype within 200 mm of shelf width, made from card and tape.
Investigate current storage and routines before choosing the form; one class does not establish other classes’ needs.
Any handling trial follows the classroom’s normal supervision and storage rules.

practice.prompt: Rewrite “The school needs a robot” as a useful inquiry question for a fictional problem of lost library books.
solution: Ask where and when returned books become difficult to locate.
Identify which users need to find them and what delays occur.
Investigate ways to improve tracking before deciding whether any robot is appropriate.
successCriteria: Ask where and when returned books become difficult to locate.
Identify which users need to find them and what delays occur.
Investigate ways to improve tracking before deciding whether any robot is appropriate.

practice.prompt: Two users report difficulty; a brief says “All users hate the product.” Correct the evidence claim.
solution: Two users reported a specific difficulty.
The evidence does not establish every user’s experience or hatred.
Record the difficulty accurately and investigate its frequency with a broader suitable sample.
successCriteria: Two users reported a specific difficulty.
The evidence does not establish every user’s experience or hatred.
Record the difficulty accurately and investigate its frequency with a broader suitable sample.

checklist: I describe a task and difficulty.

notes.title: Problem identification in context
paragraphs: A design problem describes a gap between a user’s current experience and a desired outcome. It should identify who is affected, in what situation and with what observable difficulty. Avoid turning the first proposed solution into the problem itself: “we need an app” does not explain the unmet need. Separate direct observations from interpretations about motives. A small sample can reveal a useful issue without proving that every user experiences it. A bounded brief makes constraints visible and gives later evaluation a clear purpose.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional observations: five of eight pupils leave worksheets in the wrong collection tray; two trays have similar labels. Write a problem statement.
steps: Identify users and task: pupils submitting worksheets need to distinguish the correct tray.
State the observed difficulty and limit: five of eight observed submissions were misplaced, and similar labels are a possible cause to investigate.
workedExamples.conclusion: The brief concerns reliable worksheet submission; it does not prematurely require a digital system.

flashcards.front: What makes a problem user-centred?
flashcards.back: It describes a user, situation and unmet need.

flashcards.front: Why is “build an app” not a full problem statement?
flashcards.back: It names a solution without establishing the difficulty.

flashcards.front: How should a possible cause be phrased?
flashcards.back: As a hypothesis to investigate unless evidence already establishes it.

flashcards.front: What does a bounded brief include?
flashcards.back: The need, intended users, context and relevant constraints.

lessons.summary: Choose research that answers a design question and supports a decision.
explanation: Research reduces uncertainty before design decisions. Observation can reveal where users hesitate during a task; interviews explore reasons and priorities; inspecting a comparable product can reveal construction or interaction choices. These methods answer different questions. A preference poll cannot show that a task is completed successfully. Secondary research needs an identifiable source, date and relevance to the actual context, rather than an unsupported image or copied claim.

Plan an appropriate investigation around a specific question. For classroom practice use supplied fictional records or a teacher-approved activity rather than collecting unnecessary personal information. Record observations separately from interpretations, include contradictory evidence and avoid questions that suggest the desired answer. Synthesise findings into evidence, implication, possible requirement and remaining uncertainty. A convenience sample of classmates may miss the needs of younger pupils, visitors or people with different access requirements.
keyIdeas: Method choice follows the research question.
Conflicting findings are useful evidence.
A finding should inform a decision.

definitions.meaning: Evidence gathered directly for the current investigation.
Existing information produced for another purpose.
A systematic influence that can distort evidence or its interpretation.

method: Name the decision and uncertainty.
Choose an appropriate method and participants or sources.
Use neutral prompts and record context.
Link findings to provisional requirements and limitations.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical question: why do visitors miss the library return point? Choose two methods.
steps: Observe a return task without pointing out the route, recording pauses and requests for help.
Afterwards ask what information visitors looked for and expected.
Compare actions with explanations; remembered accounts can differ from behaviour.
Use supplied anonymous notes in classroom practice and record context and sample limits.
workedExample.conclusion: Task observations and neutral follow-up questions provide complementary evidence, not automatic proof of cause.

misconceptions.mistake: Asking “Would you like our clearer new sign?”
misconceptions.correction: Ask what the person noticed without praising a proposed design.

misconceptions.mistake: Discarding a contradictory comment.
misconceptions.correction: Preserve it and investigate whether it reveals a different need.

practice.prompt: To investigate whether a paper timetable can be read from a pupil’s usual seat, choose between observing a reading task and asking which colour looks nicest. Explain.
hints: Match evidence to the intended claim.
solution: Observe the pupil reading specified entries from the usual seat under normal lighting.
Colour preference does not establish legibility; record viewing conditions and errors.

practice.prompt: Rewrite the leading question “Don’t you agree our organiser is much easier?” and explain an advantage of the replacement.
hints: Ask without suggesting the desired conclusion.
solution: After the task ask: “What, if anything, made it difficult to find the item?”
This allows difficulty, no difficulty or an unexpected issue rather than inviting agreement with “easier”.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical notes: three pupils want more colour; two cannot distinguish colour-only tray labels; all five identify written labels correctly in one classroom trial. Propose a requirement and follow-up without claiming universal accessibility.
hints: Prioritise task access and retain the sample limit.
solution: Use readable written labels as well as colour so colour is not the only identifier.
Test them in the intended position with a broader range of relevant users and lighting conditions.
The five-person trial supports a prototype choice; it does not certify accessibility for everyone.

practice.prompt: Improve “Wouldn’t a larger button be much better?” as an interview question.
solution: Ask: “How did you decide where to press?”
Follow with: “Was any part difficult to identify?”
These questions allow the user to describe the problem before proposing a button size.
successCriteria: Ask: “How did you decide where to press?”
Follow with: “Was any part difficult to identify?”
These questions allow the user to describe the problem before proposing a button size.

practice.prompt: A designer uses one old product review as proof that current users need a feature. Evaluate.
hints: Ask what current evidence is missing.
solution: The review records one person’s experience at a particular time.
The product and user context may differ from the present brief.
Use it as a lead for current user research rather than conclusive proof.
successCriteria: The review records one person’s experience at a particular time.
The product and user context may differ from the present brief.
Use it as a lead for current user research rather than conclusive proof.

checklist: I trace a finding to a decision.

notes.title: Research in context
paragraphs: Design research should answer decisions the brief actually requires. Observation can reveal what users do, while an interview can explore how they explain their experience; neither automatically replaces the other. Product analysis can identify existing approaches, but copying an attractive feature without understanding its context is weak evidence. Record source, date, method and limitations so findings can be traced. Prefer questions that invite an account of behaviour over leading questions that seek agreement. Collect only information needed for the design task and avoid recording unnecessary personal details.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional inquiry: users struggle to locate a timetable on a club noticeboard. Plan two complementary research methods.
steps: Observe a small group attempting to find a specified meeting time, recording search paths and completion.
Ask afterwards which labels or visual cues they expected, without suggesting that a particular colour is the answer.
workedExamples.conclusion: Observation reveals task behaviour; the follow-up interview helps explain expectations while remaining a self-report.

flashcards.front: What can observation reveal?
flashcards.back: Actions and difficulties during a task.

flashcards.front: What can an interview add?
flashcards.back: A user’s explanation, expectations and priorities.

flashcards.front: What is a leading question?
flashcards.back: A question that steers the respondent towards a preferred answer.

flashcards.front: Why record research limitations?
flashcards.back: They define how far the finding can support a design decision.

lessons.summary: Translate evidence into requirements that can be tested fairly.
objectives: Plan a matching test for each criterion.
explanation: A specification turns a brief and research into requirements for judging a design. “Attractive” or “easy to use” leaves the test undefined. A useful requirement identifies a property or task, a threshold, conditions and a reason. For a hypothetical tray, “external width no more than 180 mm to fit the measured shelf” can be checked with a ruler. User-task criteria also need a clear definition of success and of any permitted help.

Choose thresholds because they serve the brief, not because a finished prototype happens to meet them. Mark essential constraints separately from desirable improvements. A product that breaches a mandatory size limit cannot be rescued by a high appearance score. Record units, measurement equipment or task instructions. Requirements can change when evidence changes, but document the reason and re-evaluate rather than quietly lowering a target after a failed test.
keyIdeas: A criterion needs an observable pass condition.
Mandatory constraints cannot be averaged away.
Set thresholds before evaluation.

definitions.meaning: A set of justified requirements for a solution.
An observable condition for deciding whether a requirement is met.
A recorded link from need to requirement, design choice and evidence.

method: Extract a need or constraint from evidence.
State threshold, units and conditions.
Identify mandatory and desirable requirements.
Choose a test and record the rationale.

workedExample.prompt: A hypothetical shelf is 200 mm wide. The brief reserves 10 mm clearance on each side. Specify the maximum tray width and a test.
steps: Available width = 200 − 10 − 10 = 180 mm.
The finished tray’s greatest external width must be at most 180 mm.
Measure the widest point with a suitable ruler and record the reading.
Depth, height and stability need separate criteria.
workedExample.conclusion: Maximum width is 180 mm; passing this test alone does not establish complete suitability.

misconceptions.mistake: Writing “small enough”.
misconceptions.correction: Include a dimension and testable limit.

misconceptions.mistake: Lowering a target just to pass.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the failure; justify revised requirements and retest transparently.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical label must be found by at least four of five first-time trial users within 20 seconds without hints. Identify the threshold, conditions and success measure.
solution: Success means locating the correct label within 20 seconds.
At least four of five users must succeed; they are first-time users and receive no hints.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical shelf is 260 mm wide and needs 15 mm clearance on each side. Find the maximum organiser width and decide whether a 234 mm prototype passes.
solution: Maximum width = 260 − 15 − 15 = 230 mm.
234 mm exceeds the limit by 4 mm, so it fails.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical design has a mandatory £12 cost ceiling. Prototype A costs £14 and scores 5/5 for appearance; B costs £11 and scores 3/5. Can A be selected simply because its average score is higher? Propose a next step.
hints: A mandatory gate differs from a preference.
solution: No: A breaches the mandatory cost ceiling; appearance cannot cancel that constraint.
Consider B if it meets other mandatory requirements, or revise A’s materials and recalculate cost.
If the budget changes, record authorisation and reason rather than assuming the limit disappeared.

practice.prompt: A 300 mm opening needs 12 mm clearance on each side. Calculate the maximum object width.
solution: Total clearance is 2 × 12 = 24 mm.
Maximum width is 300 − 24 = 276 mm.
Specify an assembled width no greater than 276 mm under the stated brief.
successCriteria: Specify an assembled width no greater than 276 mm under the stated brief.

practice.prompt: Improve “The instructions must be clear” using a fictional test of five first-time users.
hints: Name a task and a threshold.
solution: A possible specification is: at least four of five first-time users complete the three-step setup without hints.
Observe the defined task using the same instructions.
Record each completion and any help rather than relying only on users saying the text is clear.
successCriteria: A possible specification is: at least four of five first-time users complete the three-step setup without hints.
Observe the defined task using the same instructions.
Record each completion and any help rather than relying only on users saying the text is clear.

checklist: I specify how to collect evidence.

notes.title: Specifications in context
paragraphs: A specification translates a need into a requirement that can be checked. State the feature or performance, threshold, conditions and method of verification. Separate mandatory constraints from preferences so a strong optional feature cannot conceal a critical failure. Include units where a quantity is measured and define ambiguous words such as easy or durable. Thresholds should come from the brief, research or a justified design decision, not be invented after seeing results. Keep the same requirement version attached to its test record.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional brief: a display must fit a 240 mm shelf with 15 mm clearance at each side. Write a maximum-width requirement.
steps: Total reserved clearance is 15 + 15 = 30 mm.
Maximum display width is 240 − 30 = 210 mm; measure the widest point after assembly.
workedExamples.conclusion: The assembled display must be no wider than 210 mm, checked with a suitable ruler at its widest point.

flashcards.front: What makes a requirement testable?
flashcards.back: A defined feature, threshold, conditions and check.

flashcards.front: Why distinguish mandatory and preferred requirements?
flashcards.back: An optional advantage cannot compensate for violating a mandatory constraint.

flashcards.front: When should thresholds be set?
flashcards.back: Before testing, using the brief or justified research.

flashcards.front: Why include units?
flashcards.back: They make quantities unambiguous and comparable.
